title: AI Dividends and Workflow Training: Live with Legora and Harbor at TLTF
author: Kyle Poe · Zena Applebaum

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source excerpt contains only closing banter, thanks, promotional requests and a music credit. It offers no substantive claims or evidence with which to assess the cluster’s proposition that legal AI benefits depend on organisational adaptation and human control.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts the competence risk: inexperienced associates may be unable to verify confident AI output, while traditional training is already uneven. It materially extends the cluster by proposing practice-specific workflows that deliberately combine human drafting, AI review, controlled output checking, explanatory playbooks and protected experimentation, although these are reported practices and predictions rather than measured learning outcomes.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship

kp.k: Client portals support collaborative, productized legal service delivery
kp.d: Kyle Poe describes the announced Legora Portal as enabling law firms to share workflows and documents and collaborate with clients who need not themselves subscribe. He frames this as infrastructure for firms reconsidering service packaging and pricing as AI accelerates delivery. His example of due diligence shrinking from three weeks to hours is an illustrative vendor claim, not a reported measured study.
qs: The firm needs to be a customer of Legora, but the client does not.
You know, for example, a due diligence might have taken three weeks in the past.
But now thanks to AI, where you can accelerate that workflow into a matter of hours, now clients expect the turnaround time to also be similarly responsive.
So as you rethink the packaging and pricing, we need technologies that can support that new form of delivery.

kp.k: Clients expect an AI dividend from outside counsel
kp.d: Poe reports that clients increasingly ask about AI in RFPs and expect savings from its use, while retaining some concerns. He argues that corporate budget dynamics can make law firms better positioned to invest than in-house departments, leading corporate counsel to look to outside firms for AI-enabled services. These are his market observations rather than quantified buyer evidence.
qs: they’re asking in RFPs, they’re asking their law firms, what are you doing in terms of AI?
They want to see some savings ⁓ from the delivery of legal services using AI.
And so in-house counsel is looking to their firms
to make those investments in AI and then deliver new legal services using those AIs.

kp.k: Legal engineers provide intensive, practice-specific implementation support
kp.d: Poe describes AI enablement as a high-touch process. Legora hires former practicing attorneys, typically with three to seven years of experience, as legal engineers who work with knowledge management and innovation teams to identify two to three high-impact use cases per practice, deliver on-site onboarding, and help individual lawyers develop prompts and workflows. Whether the firm or vendor identifies initial use cases depends on the firm's AI maturity and internal resources.
qs: AI enablement is really a high touch process, right?
these are former practicing attorneys, like typically three to seven year timeframe
We typically will work with knowledge management, innovation departments to identify two to three use cases, which we think are going to be high impact for that practice area.
they work one-on-one oftentimes with the practicing attorneys.

kp.k: Training should address entire workflows rather than isolated tasks
kp.d: Host Greg Lambert reports his firm's attorney-development team's interest in teaching process improvement rather than isolated tasks, illustrating this with meeting action items that now take minutes to edit instead of an hour to create. Zena Applebaum argues that workflow training must identify automation opportunities and review points; associates need to experience the process at least once. She predicts that integrated applications will increasingly generate workflow-level efficiency gains.
qs: And what used to take an hour to create now takes a few minutes just to edit.
So what is the workflow? What are you trying to accomplish? What is the output you want to create?
they need to go through the process, at least once to know where those places are
Particularly as integrations increase too and we start to be able to connect different applications to one another, you’re going to start to see those workflows really impact firm efficiency.

kp.k: Immediate value builds adoption habits and enables experimentation
kp.d: Poe argues that both associates and partners must develop habits around when AI adds value. Initial use cases should produce immediate benefits because an unsuitable first task can discourage further use and lawyers are not paid to beta-test software. He distinguishes grassroots workflow construction by technologically engaged associates from top-down efforts to productize firm knowledge.
qs: you have to develop some muscle memory when to use AI and when not to when it will add value to the process.
they ask you to do something it’s not really capable of doing, they get a bad experience and they never touch it again
attorneys don’t get paid to experiment with software or beta test software.
How can they productize their knowledge and experience?

kp.k: Reusable workflows convert precedent libraries into drafting support
kp.d: Poe describes an interrogatory-response workflow he created using prior discovery responses for a defendant in repeat product-liability litigation. Uploading new interrogatories allows AI to search previous answers and reuse or substantively rewrite them. He claims this provides a drafting head start and can improve quality by locating material that manual searches miss; no comparative performance measurements are supplied.
qs: a great example of workflow that I created was an interrogatory response generator
I can just upload the interrogatory requests and the AI will search through those prior responses and find if that question has been answered before.
And so it’s able to do a, oftentimes a better job than I could have done manually in terms of finding a, from the large corpus of prior responses, previous questions.

kp.k: Continuous training requires protected time beyond implementation
kp.d: Applebaum reports seeing firm announcements that set aside associate time for AI experimentation, qualifying Poe's account of limited incentives to experiment. She recommends ongoing training and adoption support as use cases and utilization change, rather than restricting education to initial implementation. She supplies no firm names or prevalence estimates.
qs: We are starting to see firms make announcements that they’re saving associate time.
And by saving, I mean putting aside associate time to experiment with AI.
there’s really this opportunity to not limit training to the implementation phase, but to make sure that you’re training throughout the use
it’s perpetual training and perpetual adoption that happens throughout time as the use cases change

kp.k: Junior lawyers need explicit preparation for checking AI output
kp.d: Lambert cautions against assuming young associates understand AI. Reporting a previous guest's observation, he says recent law graduates had been discouraged from using it on ethics grounds. He recommends beginning with subjects the user knows well enough to assess results because AI sounds confident whether correct or not, and inexperienced associates may lack the knowledge needed to check it.

just this group over the past three years that have come out of law school has basically been told, don’t use AI because it might be a violation of the ethics code
you need to use something that you’re an expert in so that you can evaluate the results that you’re getting back.
Because it sounds super confident, whether it’s right or wrong.

kp.k: Training can alternate human drafting and AI-assisted review
kp.d: Poe describes clinic educators resisting complete automation because students still need to learn underlying work. He proposes playbooks that review manually drafted student or associate work, alongside AI drafting followed by human review, and predicts better-prepared associates in a year or two as clinic adoption grows. Applebaum separately reports controlled firm exercises in which learners review AI-generated output, emphasizing integrity rather than reliance on AI alone.
qs: you can have the AI draft in a human review, or you can have a human draft in AI review.
the associates should be more trained in like a year or two, because we’re starting to see a lot of traction in the law school clinic program.
we want to train these people to actually do the work themselves.
And they do this in a very controlled environment.
And you’re not just relying on the AI.

kp.k: Explanatory AI feedback could supplement uneven associate mentoring
kp.d: Poe argues that traditional associate training is inconsistent and dependent on access to mentors, drawing on his experience of receiving unexplained redlines. He proposes using AI to explain revisions and codified contract playbooks to provide rationales for changes, claiming that this can support both training and verification. This is his proposed benefit, not demonstrated verification accuracy. Applebaum cautions that associates must actively engage with such opportunities.
qs: Not all associates get equal opportunities for advancement and training in firms.
I just got redline changes back from briefs was writing, and there was no explanations.
you get not just red lines back, but you get actually at a rationale like an explanation of every single change.
It solves both the training problem and the verification problem because it’s showing its work.
It puts a lot of onus on the associate though to want to engage in that way.

kp.k: AI disruption will differ across practices and influence acquisitions
kp.d: In the closing forecast, Poe expects greater adoption but uneven effects across tasks and practice areas, including resistance from more threatened practices. He reports managing partners considering how AI changes acquisition strategy: assessing a team requires anticipating its practice's exposure over the next 16 or 18 months, not simply evaluating current performance. These are expectations and reported strategic questions, not established restructuring outcomes.

kp.k: Future commercial change requires costly data and infrastructure preparation
kp.d: Applebaum expresses hope that AI will materially change legal practice and commercial models, rather than presenting that outcome as established. She recommends immediate operational planning for benefits three to five years ahead, particularly investment in IT, cloud infrastructure, and organizing firm data. She argues that firms have not necessarily connected these preparatory costs with future opportunities.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The speakers describe AI-driven changes to advisory demand, service delivery, workflow efficiency, training and law-firm strategy.
pts.d: Sam Moore (00:20) reports increased requests from law firms for assistance advising clients on AI strategy, compliance and regulation. Kyle Poe (06:13–09:18) presents Legora Portal as a means of sharing workflows, documents and interactive diligence with clients; he claims AI can compress an illustrative diligence workflow from three weeks to hours, raising expectations for responsiveness. He reports firms considering productized legal services and clients seeking an 'AI dividend' through savings, with in-house counsel often looking to firms to invest. Zena Applebaum (15:01) predicts that efficiency gains will increasingly come from whole workflows rather than isolated tasks, especially as applications become integrated. Poe (16:52) describes a reusable interrogatory-response workflow that searches prior responses and drafts answers, claiming it can save time and find relevant precedents better than manual searching. Applebaum (20:17) reports firms reserving associate time for AI experimentation and moving toward continuing training. Poe (22:45–27:33) proposes AI-assisted review and explanations of redlines as training tools, and claims explanations can also support verification; Applebaum describes controlled exercises in reviewing AI output rather than simply relying on it. Poe (28:22) claims general AI advances reach legal AI within weeks. Looking ahead, Poe (29:47) predicts increased adoption but uneven effects and resistance across practices, including implications for acquisitions. Applebaum (30:56) expresses hope that practice changes will influence commercial models and argues that firms need substantial IT and data investment to benefit.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists primarily of commercial implementation experience, personal practice experience, reported client conversations and unnamed firm examples, rather than systematic measurements.
pts.d: Moore's demand claim rests on requests received by Legal Technology Hub. Poe speaks as a Legora employee about its product capabilities, client reactions and onboarding practices, including legal engineers working with knowledge management and innovation teams to select practice-specific use cases. His interrogatory example is a workflow he says he created, informed by his product-liability practice experience; no measured comparison of speed, retrieval accuracy or output quality is supplied. The three-weeks-to-hours diligence claim is illustrative, without a specified matter, sample or benchmark. His training argument draws on personal experience receiving unexplained redlines and on work with law-school clinics. Applebaum's adoption and training claims refer to unnamed firm announcements and controlled review exercises, without adoption figures or learning-outcome measures. Poe's forecast about acquisitions references conversations with managing partners. His claim of rapid diffusion cites GPT-5 being used roughly a week after release, without identifying the deployment. The transcript offers no systematic study, benchmark or quantified return-on-investment analysis for these claims; the future efficiency and commercial-model statements are predictions or expectations.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current adoption claims are qualified by implementation and training requirements; forecasts range from weeks to five years.
pts.d: In this 2025 interview, Poe describes the portal as announced the previous week; access requires the law firm, but not its client, to be a Legora customer. Current workflow benefits depend on choosing suitable tasks, developing habitual use and demonstrating immediate value: Poe warns that an initial request beyond a tool's capabilities can discourage further use. Applebaum conditions broader efficiency gains on workflow redesign and increasing integrations. Both stress training beyond initial implementation, including understanding the underlying work and reviewing output. Poe predicts better-prepared associates in approximately one or two years as law-school clinic engagement grows. His training-and-verification claim is expressly conditional on proper use and deliberate workflow design; AI explanations are presented as a support layer, not accompanied by a demonstrated accuracy guarantee. Applebaum adds that associates must actively engage. Poe describes general-to-legal AI diffusion as taking weeks. In response to a question about the next few months to a year, he predicts adoption and practice-specific disruption, and says acquisition decisions should consider AI's effects over the next 16–18 months. Applebaum's operational investment argument has a three-to-five-year horizon, with preparation needed immediately; material commercial-model change is expressed as a hope without a firm date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The discussion principally concerns law firms, corporate legal buyers, associates and legal-technology implementation teams, with uneven impacts across practices.
pts.d: Moore describes clients across sectors needing legal advice about AI deployment. Poe identifies corporate clients and in-house counsel as buyers expecting savings, faster responses and greater participation in legal workflows, while often depending on outside firms to fund AI capabilities. Law firms face changes to service packaging, pricing, reusable knowledge products and acquisition strategy. Knowledge management and innovation teams work with Legora's legal engineers—described as former practicing attorneys—to identify use cases and support adoption; firms with leaner internal teams may depend more on vendor assistance. Associates and partners must learn where AI adds value. Associates and law students are also affected through changing training methods: human drafting with AI review, or AI drafting followed by human review, rather than unquestioned direct reliance on output. Poe argues that AI explanations could supplement uneven access to partner mentoring; Applebaum expects benefits to depend on individual engagement. Managing partners face differing returns, threats and resistance across practices, while operational leaders must prepare data and IT infrastructure. The transcript does not make a concrete claim about lawyer headcount reductions or improved access to justice.
